style: independent intraday futures trader; supply/demand + volume profile + stats
edge_principles: Track rule-following errors before tracking P&L stats: stats on trades that break your rules are random noise; removing error trades alone moved him from losing to slightly positive
Keep a rolling stat sheet (~20 market stats, ~1500-day window, refreshed monthly) and only use stats above ~65% that also carry meaningful profit potential
A high-probability stat (e.g. one side of the initial balance breaks) is context or a target, not an entry; it needs an entry and a risk-reward to be an edge
Use maximum adverse excursion of past 'successful' stat outcomes to decide where to enter and when to abandon the stat
Skip trades whose reward to first target is under 1.5R; score trades 1.5-2R as OK and above 2R as high quality
Fixed fractional risk per trade: widen stop -> shrink size
Build long/neutral/short scenarios from 60-min and 15-min charts pre-market; redraw mini-plans several times a day
Grade every trade (in plan?, played to win vs not lose, patience, R:R, entry, exit) and review weekly with repeated 'why' questions
notes: Process/stats-focused episode. Main concrete rule is a size-banded gap-fill fade entered at the historical MAE zone; rest is planning and review discipline.

style: retail momentum day trader, ~90% short low-priced stocks
edge_principles: Keep position size small while learning; small size is what let him survive seven losing years
Scale into shorts rather than one full-size entry, so a front-side short that keeps running is survivable
Track daily P&L curve and ask before each trade whether it is good enough to affect the curve; skip substandard setups
Maintain a curated watchlist of repeat runners ('pig list') so no research is needed when one moves again
Shorting the backside (after the high fails) is safer than shorting the front side of a run
Accountability (public P&L) reduced overtrading and impatience
notes: Mostly a career story. One setup: shorting gapping junk microcaps from a pre-built list, ideally on the backside after VWAP loss or failed high.

style: systematic multi-strategy fund (China futures)
edge_principles: Classify strategies as divergent (trend: many small losses, fat right tail) or convergent (mean reversion: high win rate, fat left tail) by their return histogram, and mix both

Treat each strategy's P&L as a tradable return series; allocate across strategies by correlation and risk-adjusted return, rebalance quarterly, let weights go to zero rather than hand-picking retirements
Diversify on three axes: strategy family, timeframe/parameter set, and market; trade a family of parameter sets instead of one optimised parameter
Hypothesis-first research beats data mining; stop at models you can still open up and explain
Test strategies on synthetic series with known trend and noise levels to see how much noise they tolerate, especially when real history is short
Daily statistical-process-control overlay to switch off a strategy that stops behaving like its backtest
Discretionary traders should define their pattern precisely, collect all examples, and execute it the same way each time to remove self-induced performance noise
Reduce leverage/volatility once the annual target is met
notes: Portfolio-construction and research-process episode; no concrete single setup.

style: prop / independent momentum day trader
markets: US small caps, biotech, IPOs, OTC stocks; formerly bitcoin
edge_principles: Keep a varied playbook (parabolic shorts, hot IPOs, mid-cap earnings breakouts, long and short) because themes and order flow rotate in and out of fashion
Go where the unusual volume and attention are; edges dry up when order flow leaves a theme
Execution/liquidity risk can turn a planned 1R loss into ~3R on illiquid names; size for exit liquidity, not just stop distance
Being consistently green by scalping small profits is not enough; the money is in holding the open-to-close move once the turning point confirms
A prop firm with a 50/50-style split and no deposit has an incentive to develop traders; a deposit requirement and tiny firm cut signal a churn model
Group-think inside a trading room causes crowded entries that get stopped out together
notes: Ex-poker player turned momentum trader. Setups are mostly discretionary (parabolic junk shorts timed intraday, open-to-close trend capture with VWAP trail); an old pre-market OTC pricing glitch is historical only.

style: merchant energy trader / hedge fund PM; fundamental relationship and spread trading
markets: electricity, natural gas, crude oil (physical and futures)
edge_principles: Always know your exact position; reconcile the system position yourself
Trade relationships (calendar spreads, location basis, heat rates, frac spreads) rather than outright price levels
Size mean-reversion positions small enough to survive further multi-SD excursions before reverting
Fundamental trades need enough capital/risk budget to sit through noise; under-capitalised traders get chopped out before the thesis plays out
Short-term and long-term fundamentals are different skill sets; don't assume a good short-tenor trader will transfer to term trading
Treat independent trading as an actual business, not a hobby
notes: Energy merchant-desk career. Ideas are futures spread / term-structure trades, not testable with MCF stock data.

style: independent high-frequency discretionary day trader (OTC penny stocks, later Nasdaq)
markets: US OTC bulletin board stocks, later Nasdaq small caps
edge_principles: Find a niche and master it; trade where you compete with uninformed participants rather than well-resourced funds
Review results by instrument/type and cut whatever consistently loses (he dropped ETFs and large caps)
An edge from market structure eventually disappears; press size while it lasts but have a plan for when it ends
When moving to a new market, restart with small size: prior skill does not transfer automatically
Hard daily max-loss stop; do not let a green day turn red
After a big loss rebuild with small trades and a few green days before restoring size; after a big win also return to base size (avoid the 'makeup trade' of doubling after a winner)
If you get shaken out, you were sized too big
Measure progress by streaks of green days (consistency), not by dollar targets
Hold ~2 years of expenses and prove profitability before trading full time
notes: Career and psychology episode; his OTC pattern (reported ~85% directional accuracy, several overnight holds a day) is never specified, so no testable setup was extracted.

style: retail swing/trend trader on daily charts; entrepreneur
edge_principles: Beginners should avoid low-timeframe day trading; lower-timeframe stops sit inside higher-timeframe chop
Accept a low win rate (~32%) when payoffs are small losses, small wins and occasional very large wins; one or two 1000-pip trends make the year
Probe entries at 0.25% risk; add (0.5-0.75%) only once the trade is ~100 pips in profit
Make trade management mechanical (EMA trail) to avoid snatching profits while watching P&L
If you must think about a setup for more than a few seconds, skip it
After time away from markets, trade small until your read is back
Stop runs through obvious support/resistance are where large players get filled; expect overshoots
notes: Daily-chart FX trend catcher: anticipatory limit entries at second test of key levels and range edges, scale-in, and a two-stage 8/21 EMA trailing stop. Remainder is business/education talk.

style: academic (Harvard Business School); white-collar crime research
edge_principles: Legal information edges exist through costly alternative data (card spend, satellite parking-lot counts) rather than misappropriated information; MCF must stay on the legal side of data sourcing
Returns that are too smooth (consistent ~8-12% with no drawdowns) are a red flag for any manager or strategy
Companies can manage reported earnings through reserve and pension assumptions; earnings beats are not always operational
notes: Interview on white-collar crime (Madoff, insider trading definitions, earnings management). No trading setups.

style: quant at HFT futures firm; systematic strategy data-miner (Build Alpha)
edge_principles: Escaping randomness: every rule tweak after a few losses resets you to trade zero; let an edge run enough trades before judging it
Require a minimum trade count per rule (his rule of thumb: ~500 trades per rule, e.g. 3 rules -> 1500 trades)
Use out-of-sample (default ~35%) plus rotating cross-validation; note that changing the OOS window changes which strategies survive
Prefer non-parametric/counting conditions (consecutive higher highs, consecutive down closes) over optimised look-back lengths; use look-back indicators only as fixed regime filters
Volume and volatility regimes give context for expectations
Monte Carlo reshuffle the trade list: a backtest equity curve is often near the top of the distribution, so set live expectations from the distribution, not the single curve
Variance testing: re-simulate with a lower win rate (e.g. 61% -> 55%) to check the strategy survives degraded performance
Prefer asymmetric payoff (bigger wins than losses) because live results degrade versus backtest
Size all bets equally within a strategy so no single trade dominates; maximise number of independent trades (law of large numbers), net of costs
Logical sense of a mined strategy raises confidence after the fact
notes: Research-methodology episode directly relevant to MCF lab rules (OOS, trade counts, Monte Carlo, variance tests). No concrete setup disclosed.

style: retail aggressive small-cap short seller (~99% short)
edge_principles: Small-account growth came from consistent small daily gains in one well-known setup, not from big swings
Short-sale-restriction (SSR) days plus tiny float can produce extreme squeezes because shorts cannot hit bids; avoid or size down
Lack of a predefined max loss and adding to losers produced his worst days; he now stops half the position automatically
With a small account, only short after the reversal is confirmed; probing early is only affordable with a large account
Wait for high-quality setups even if that means trading only a few days a week
Holding a confirmed fader for 2-3 days captures the 'easy money' after the crowd moves on
notes: Main setup: short low-quality sympathy plays of a sector runner once the lead stock reverses, hold through multi-day fade; partial overnight holds when below VWAP into close.

style: fund (sports-betting hedge fund, quant models + in-play trading)
markets: sports betting exchanges (football, cricket, golf, tennis, racing)
edge_principles: Size each trade relative to the liquidity of the specific event so you can always exit; avoid thin markets entirely
Only trade with a clear model premium (he requires the market price ~25% better than model fair value); cherry-pick a few of many available markets
Hedge out/lock in as soon as the favourable move happens; holding a position that won't move further for 30 minutes is risk without reward
Typical risk 1.5% (max 3%) of capital per trade, with typical realised loss a fraction of that thanks to in-play hedging
Skip events dominated by unquantifiable qualitative factors even when the model shows value
Markets tend to overreact to sudden news (e.g. player injuries); that can be an opportunity
Track volatility and number of negative months, not just total return
notes: Sports betting fund; principles on liquidity-relative sizing, value thresholds and fast profit-locking transfer to MCF. Setup is not stock-testable.

style: hedge fund execution/prop trader (Galleon, Argus); author
edge_principles: Write down, while calm, the price at which you would buy (and why); when price gets there and the fundamentals have not changed, act despite the bad tape
Look for the second-order beneficiary/victim of news (the stock whose earnings depend on the news), not just the headline name
Impaired state (hangover, no sleep) degrades execution; don't trade when not at 100%
notes: Memoir episode on hedge-fund culture, sell-side entertainment, insider-trading era and addiction. Trade anecdotes are information-driven and not systematic; no testable setup.

style: former CBOE floor options market maker; options education/systems
markets: US equity and index options, FX options
edge_principles: After a large drawdown, cut to minimum size (one lot) and rebuild with a small fixed daily target; scale back up only after consistent results
Package option positions into defined-risk spreads (verticals, butterflies, calendars) so risk is finite and easy to read ('staying spread is staying alive')
Map spread values across a grid of time, price and volatility before trading so reactions are pre-computed
A volatility move can make a directionally right position lose (long premium crushed by implied vol drop)
Discipline = keep the plan's risk and size guidelines unchanged mid-trade; otherwise you cannot tell whether the plan or the deviation caused the result
Set a realistic daily objective and stop swinging for home runs once it's reached
notes: Options market-maker career; lessons are about spreads, vol risk and rebuilding after losses. No intraday stock setup.

style: independent cross-asset 'high-velocity' macro trader; regime-based strategy allocation
markets: ~35 futures markets (ags, metals, rates, indices) and options
edge_principles: The edge is not the individual systems (MA cross, RSI) but deciding which strategy family to lever up or down for the current regime
Assess regime on three axes: technical, fundamental, sentiment (including positioning)
Judge performance as return per unit of risk (his 'Netto number'), not raw return
Prefer a smooth equity curve of small, compounding gains over lumpy outcomes; smooth curves can be levered
Small capital is an advantage: trade edges too small for large funds
Grade yourself daily on preparation, routine, focus, plan execution and adaptation
Being slightly uncomfortable in a trade is normal for asymmetric trades; overconfidence leads to complacency
notes: Macro futures trader; the one rule-like idea is choosing momentum vs mean-reversion strategies depending on whether a scheduled data release surprises.

style: quant / hedge fund (convertible and warrant hedging, statistical arbitrage); gambling theorist
edge_principles: Edge = mathematical expectation per unit of action; bet big when the edge is present and small or not at all when it isn't
Kelly sizing: bet roughly edge divided by variance; it maximises long-run growth, betting the whole bankroll leads to ruin; fractional Kelly if the horizon or estimates are uncertain
In markets probabilities are only estimated; take trades where even the pessimistic scenario still looks favourable
Hedge away the main risk factor (e.g. stock price) to isolate a mispricing (warrant vs stock delta hedge)
Two jobs: find an edge (hard) and manage the bankroll (solved by Kelly-type rules)
Find a game that suits your abilities; edges differ by person and change over time
Passive indexing beats most investors with no work
notes: Card-counting and warrant-hedging pioneer; principles on edge definition and Kelly sizing. No intraday setup.

style: retail/independent momentum swing trader (O'Neil/Minervini/Morales style)
edge_principles: Pick one asset class and style; style drift (e.g. day trading the index while running a stock swing book) costs focus and money
Do not chase: skip the trade if price is more than ~3-4% past the pivot
Do not cut a correctly bought trade before its stop just because it isn't working yet
Re-enter the market from cash incrementally: test with one or two leaders; if they fail, stay in cash
Judge market health by how leading stocks act, not by the index
Aim to be a '2:1' trader (avg gain ~2x avg loss at ~50% win rate); keep a scorecard of every trade and review weekly/monthly/quarterly; trimming average loss from 10% to 7% compounds strongly
Position ~6-10% of capital per stock with a stop that risks ~0.5-2% of equity; up to ~20% via adds on multiple setups
Move stop to breakeven once ~10% up; sell partials into fast extensions (e.g. +20% in a few days)
Avoid illiquid microcaps where the spread alone can hit your stop
Short only former leaders when the market is under distribution
notes: Clear daily-chart momentum setups (VCP breakout, pocket pivot, first pullback to MA, power play) with explicit chase and stop rules; testable on daily bars.

style: systematic quant (mega-cap equity mean-reversion portfolio of 9 systems)
markets: US mega-cap stocks; developing FX/futures edges
edge_principles: Define an objective function before development (e.g. positive every year, annual return as a multiple of max drawdown) and score all variants with it
Judge by max drawdown, not average drawdown; expect a worse drawdown in the future
Prefer simple rules with many degrees of freedom (his live strategy: ~12-15k data points, <50 rules); parameter neighbours should give similar results (no narrow 'ledge')
Quarantine a final out-of-sample set and look at it once; any tweak after viewing it makes it in-sample
A rule should still show positive expectancy on related markets (e.g. 10y vs 5y/30y notes, other stocks); falling apart elsewhere is a red flag
Model fills conservatively: a limit counts as filled only if price trades through it
Monitor live edge decay with rolling return, drawdown versus backtest and rolling win rate; have an answer to 'how will I know it stopped working'
Equity regimes shift (e.g. more mean reversion after 1987); expect occasional revamps
Use focused, uninterrupted research blocks
notes: Second appearance; research-methodology focus, directly relevant to MCF research rules. No setup details disclosed.

style: former options market maker (Hull Trading) and institutional delta-one/ETF trader
markets: index options, ETFs, index futures, swaps
edge_principles: Never be the biggest participant in a market; you need someone to exit to
Market-making edge = capture the spread; but watch net accumulation from one-sided order flow and cover when risk limits are crossed, accepting a small edge give-up
Know P&L under pre-set shocks (e.g. -5%, -10%) and act when tolerance is breached
For trading ETFs pick the most liquid fund (volume, options listed, borrow); for holding pick lowest fee and tracking error
A structural edge (e.g. exclusive listing/order flow) can vanish overnight; traders who relied on it alone had to leave
Retail now has far less information disadvantage; leverage is an edge only if used judiciously and sized as % of capital
notes: Pit and institutional career story plus ETF selection notes; no testable setup.

style: market-structure quant (wholesaler internalisation at UBS/Citadel/CS, IEX, Gemini bitcoin exchange)
edge_principles: Retail marketable orders are profitable to wholesalers because they cross the spread; when MCF sends market orders it pays that spread, so prefer limit/midpoint execution where fill risk allows
Non-marketable retail limit orders are routed to exchanges chosen for rebates, not necessarily best fill quality
About 30-35% of US equity volume trades off-exchange but is included in consolidated volume
Less mature markets (early bitcoin) have more exploitable cross-venue and momentum inefficiencies because sophisticated market makers are absent
Closing auctions concentrate liquidity; indicative auction prices published before the close keep the auction near the last trade
notes: Market-structure and crypto episode; useful execution-cost context, no trading setup.

style: prop futures day trader (FUTEX, Axia Futures); order-flow and news-driven
markets: E-mini S&P, Euro Stoxx 50, Bund, US 10y, FX futures, gold, commodities
edge_principles: After a break (holiday), cut size to minimum for 1-2 weeks until timing and market feel return
Grow size by process: request ~25% higher limits monthly and push one 'all-in' (max-limit) trade per day so the larger clip becomes normal
Increase size when probability is clearly in your favour and cut back hard when conditions are poor (leverage the good, back off the bad)
Prepare scenarios for binary events (central banks, key data) with known market positioning so you react, not think
A data surprise the market refuses to follow is information: the underlying flow is the other way
Aim to execute the one good trade each day very well rather than many trades
Daily process checklist (12 boxes: arrival time, morning sheet, midday break, etc.) measures progress independent of P&L
Manage 'energy capital': schedule rest around high-volatility weeks and overnight events
Record and replay sessions in the debrief
notes: Futures day trader; concrete rule is to stop-and-reverse when a news-driven move fully retraces to its pre-news level.

style: hybrid quantitative/discretionary technical trader; research firm CIO
markets: stocks, FX, futures/commodities, options; intraday to multi-week
edge_principles: Measure any signal against the baseline drift (buy-and-hold); a system that makes 5%/yr when buy-and-hold makes 7% has negative edge
Distinguish statistical significance from economic significance: a short signal can be significantly worse than drift and still lose money
Intraday 'edges' can be bid-ask bounce; model spread and costs or the edge is fictitious
Avoid look-ahead in backtests (e.g. buying 'at the moving average' when the MA moves with the forming bar); forward test before trading
Test pattern recognition bar-by-bar at the right edge, on a different dataset than the one used to define the pattern
Mean reversion vs momentum balance differs by asset class: daily stocks mean-revert more, commodities trend more
Discretion must be bounded: position size is never discretionary; discretion only within pre-set ranges (stop placement, take/skip)
Struggling trader framework: stop trading, write a plan, backtest across regimes, forward test, trade tiny size, earn the right to size up through rule-following
Stock positions are highly correlated in a selloff; diversify across asset classes to smooth the curve
Adjustment period (losses) is normal when moving to a new market; budget for it
notes: Research-method episode; one concrete, testable claim: 20-day breakout works on commodities but loses on stocks.

style: prop firm CEO (T3 Trading); runs automated high/medium-frequency strategies
edge_principles: Know the downside of every trade before entering; first losses are tuition
Forward test new automated strategies with 100-share size and real slippage rather than trusting multi-year backtests
Run every live strategy in parallel in a paper 'test broker' with the same slippage model and compare to calibrate costs
Budget double the expected time to get a system working and enough capital to survive early losses, costs and living expenses
Be conservative on slippage, spread, commissions and market impact; most retail-built systems fail on these and on overfitting
Short-hold momentum scalping is now dominated by machines; discretionary traders should lengthen holding periods (e.g. hours)
Strategies often work only at certain times of day (some fail in the volatile open, some work only in the last minutes); test by time-of-day bucket
Keep small low-frequency strategies running if they are consistently positive and cost nothing extra
A firm diversified across trading styles survives regime changes; keep business cash flow positive
Many displayed bids/offers are not real liquidity; he prefers taking liquidity over passive quoting
notes: Prop firm and automation perspective; gives an example if-then rule (52-week high then pullback) only as illustration. No concrete setup with stated results.

style: former floor trader (AMEX, NYBOT orange juice), Tudor-funded trader; now CIO of a long/short equity fund
markets: futures, options, US equities (long/short ~80-100 each side, ~5-day holds)
edge_principles: Take only trades where every condition lines up (great, not merely good, trades), as when he first became consistent
When something that should happen does not happen (bullish flow or news without price follow-through), that is high-value information
Size bets by modelled probability (Thorp/Kelly-style) but always define the point where you are wrong
Faster markets compress old multi-week moves into hours; reduce size to keep risk constant
Large funded-trader programs can use aggregate trader positioning as a sentiment indicator
He takes profits too quickly; understanding why a move happens helps hold winners
Short-horizon catalyst portfolios turn over ~5 days now versus ~2 weeks 15 years ago
notes: Two concrete ideas: consolidation 'pressure point' breakouts with oscillator divergence, and fading flow that fails to move price (needs options-flow data).

style: HFT/quant fund founder (Tradeworx, MANA Partners)
markets: US equities and multi-asset quant strategies
edge_principles: Quant crowding comes from everyone using the same inputs; orthogonal (uncorrelated) data sources are what add value
Strong structural priors about how markets work beat letting ML build the whole model, especially with short alternative-data histories
Short-horizon quants net to zero impact over their holding period; long-term discretionary capital sets lasting price direction, so modelling their decision process is fruitful
HFT strategies do well in volatile conditions and complement slower quant strategies
Do not copy successful firms; look where others are not looking
notes: Business/industry episode on HFT and alternative data; no setup.

style: retail long-biased small-cap momentum day trader ('cash-flow' trading)
edge_principles: Never average down into a losing trade; it was his biggest early weakness
Place stops at structural invalidation (e.g. low of day for a long), not at a dollar amount that sits just above support

Journal every trade with time of day, setup, confidence score and emotion; filtering ~100+ trades revealed his first-15-minute trades lost ~8 of 10 times, so he now skips the first trade after the open
Journaling also showed he loses on sub-$1 stocks; cut losing categories
Size larger only on setups with a proven high confidence score; scale in (small starter, then larger at the trigger) and scale out quickly into the breakout
Adding at the breakout into a wall can turn a winner into a loser; watch late adds
No margin and ~2% risk thinking helped him avoid blowing up while learning
Most profit came in hot-sector periods; stop giving it back with off-strategy experiments in quiet periods
notes: Long-side counterpart to ep104: buy sympathy names in a hot sector on a consolidation breakout when the sector leader surges; high win-rate, quick scale-outs.

style: fund (Cambria) quantitative asset allocation; value + trend
markets: global ETFs: stocks, bonds, real assets
edge_principles: Set expectations from long history: real returns ~5% stocks, ~2% bonds, ~1% bills; 50-80% drawdowns in stocks are normal
Costs and taxes dominate long-run outcomes; a 1.25% fee can turn the best allocation into the worst
Have a written investment/trading plan and share it for accountability; sentiment extremes (most bullish Jan 2000, most bearish Mar 2009) show why
Value (cheap) plus momentum/trend (going up) is the best combination of tilts
Combine buy-and-hold and trend following 50/50 to diversify both returns and psychology
Valuation (10-year CAPE) informs multi-year expected returns, not short-term timing
notes: Long-horizon allocation episode aimed at giving active traders a passive core. Ideas are position-horizon, not intraday.

style: strategist/academic (Credit Suisse, Columbia); decision making, skill vs luck
edge_principles: In probabilistic fields judge decisions by process, not outcome; a good outcome from a bad process is still bad
Keep a decision journal (what, why, expected outcome, date, feelings) to defeat hindsight bias
Use the outside view: compare your expectation with the base rate of similar cases before acting
More information raises confidence much faster than accuracy; prioritise the few variables that matter
Use 'read-do' checklists for high-emotion moments (e.g. a position down 10% vs market) and 'do-confirm' checklists for routine
Pre-mortem: imagine the trade failed and list why, before entering
Estimate luck vs skill: var(observed) = var(skill) + var(luck); short samples are luck-dominated
Hard question: distinguishing a broken process from a normal losing streak (e.g. 15 losers in a row) needs pre-set statistical criteria
Great traders: probabilistic thinking, always positive expectancy, respect time/sample size and survival
notes: Decision-making episode; relevant to MCF rules on holdouts, expectation-setting and live monitoring. No setups.

style: electronic market maker (Virtu Financial CEO)
edge_principles: Hit singles: a ~51-52% win rate plus a large scratch rate over millions of trades yields near-daily profitability (law of large numbers)
Do not hold losing inventory hoping for mean reversion; exit at scratch or take a small loss quickly
Edges built only on speed or special access are not durable; scale and shared infrastructure across asset classes are
Heavy pre-trade and real-time post-trade risk checks (house vs street reconciliation) are worth some latency
Show a tight daily P&L distribution rather than swinging for the fences
notes: Market-making business episode; no retail-applicable setup, but the 'many small positive-expectancy trades, cut fast' principle is relevant.

style: prop futures order-flow trader and trader-development lead (Cygnet Trading)
edge_principles: Early beginner's luck is dangerous: a style that suits the current regime (e.g. buying breakouts in trending, liquid markets) fails when volatility/liquidity change
Be at your worst when trading your smallest size
Read order flow in terms of who is trapped, under pressure, fearful or greedy at important prices
Trading edges get competed away: the same P&L may need 2.5x then 10x the size years later; firms should diversify across styles/products/timeframes (casino model)
Execution matters: when working a sell order into an offered market be more aggressive, into a bid market step back
There is no fixed 'setup'; order-flow signals like absorption vary daily, so build skill rather than recipes
A trader needs a sufficient sample (not 3 trades in a trending year) across regimes before being judged
Low financial pressure while learning keeps money worries from making decisions
notes: Career and trader-development episode; no explicit rule-based setup.

style: retail small-cap scalper (avg hold 2-3 min, ~20 round trips/day)
edge_principles: Choose a style that matches your personality (he scalps because he is impatient/anxious) rather than forcing yourself into another
Use VWAP as a directional over/under: only long above VWAP, only short below; distance from VWAP indicates who controls the stock
Use limit orders only; a panic market order in a fast illiquid stock filled at the low
Hotkeys and pre-entered price levels are essential for fast execution
3-minute bars balance noise (1-min) and lag (5-min) for short holds
Most of his money is made in the open; he stops trading over the midday lull ('trader nap')
Record level 2/time and sales and replay slowly to learn tape patterns (iceberg sellers, bid props), which differ per stock
Paper trade first and start small; quit the day job only after 2 years of six-figure trading and ~5 years of savings
notes: Small-cap scalper trading top gappers with VWAP bias and tape reading; concrete universe and bias rules, entries are discretionary.

style: former options market maker; trading-industry headhunter
edge_principles: Strategy shelf lives are shrinking; the valuable skill is repeatedly finding new strategies, not owning one
Port existing ideas to new markets/products and invest selectively where you can be competitive
Manual discretionary trading margins keep shrinking; capture discretionary market knowledge in (partly) automated rules
Hiring follows volume first, volatility second; quiet low-vol periods follow crashes
notes: Careers/recruiting episode; no setups.

style: CTA business support / introducing broker (Capital Trading Group)
edge_principles: Investors judge a strategy partly on recoverability: a drawdown far beyond its historical worst is the real red flag
Expect fee compression; skin in the game matters to allocators
Know a strategy's capacity before scaling so one large allocation does not dominate
Long trends have been harder to capture since 2008 and electronic trading; option-premium strategies grew, with gap/outlier risk
notes: How to set up a CTA (track record, NFA disclosure document, compliance, marketing). No setups.

style: prop trading firm founder (Kershner Trading, CloudQuant); discretionary US equities
edge_principles: If a trade idea fails twice, rarely try it a third time

Plan risk and reward before entry (e.g. risk 1-1.5 points to make 3.5-4); his biggest losses came from not setting a hard stop when intuition said to exit (e.g. holding an earnings gap through its washout)
Ability to sit through adverse moves is both a strength and a weakness; without a structured scale-down plan winners turn into losers
Trade according to your psychology; the best traders trade large size with the same decision process as small size
Ladder into fades of extended moves in small chunks to feel the market; cut everything when clearly wrong
Prefer adding to winners over losers; new traders should not ladder at all until they have a consistent edge (win >50%, 3-4:1 payoff)
Tally mistakes daily in a journal; call out trades to peers for accountability
Use automated alerts/models to surface only setups that fit your strategy out of thousands of stocks
notes: Discretionary fader/bottom picker plus swing breakouts; a concrete earnings-gap exit lesson and laddered extreme-fade approach, not fully specified.

style: fund (ex-Salomon arb desk, LTCM founding partner; Elm Partners index investing)
markets: fixed income relative value (past); global ETFs
edge_principles: Bet sizing alone can turn a winning edge into ruin: in a 60/40 coin experiment ~30% of financially trained subjects went bust and only ~20% hit the cap
Bet a constant fraction of current capital; Kelly (edge/odds, 20% for 60/40 even money) maximises growth; something below Kelly (8-20%) is robust
Over-betting (e.g. 50% per flip) raises arithmetic expected value but produces negative median outcomes (volatility drag): six wins and four losses at 50% leaves you down ~30%
Gambler's fallacy and boredom led people to bet against a known edge
Telling a 60/40 coin from a 50/50 coin with 95% confidence takes ~143 flips; similarly, distinguishing a Sharpe 0.2 manager from 0 needs ~143 years - historical track records carry little information
Relative-value trades often have fat negative tails; size them so a tail event is survivable (LTCM lesson: a third of the positions would have survived)
notes: Bet-sizing and statistical-evidence episode; no setups. Strong support for MCF fractional sizing and skepticism toward short track records.

style: real estate investor (distressed property value-add)
markets: US real estate (Florida apartments, hotels, retail)
edge_principles: Buy distressed assets others avoid where value can be added; the worst property in a decent area
Require a minimum profit relative to capital at risk before committing (his rule of thumb: ~$1M profit on $1M purchase + $1M rehab)
Specialise in a narrow geography and asset type to build domain knowledge
Sell into strong markets without regret about leaving money on the table; buy heavily in weak markets
Thorough due diligence; speed and certainty of execution win deals
notes: Real-estate episode; no market trading setups.

style: quant / machine learning (CloudQuant; ex-Millburn, Merrill, Citadel)
edge_principles: Build in three separate stages: signal (entry only), risk allocation, trade expression (execution)
Judge a signal by win rate vs payoff ratio against the break-even win rate (2:1 payoff needs >33%); trend followers live at 25-35% win rates with ~5:1 payoffs
Mediocre signals are often dressed up with curve-fit stop/trailing rules that fail out of sample; plain P&L stops are rarely optimal, prefer a thesis-invalidated exit
Start allocation from an equal-weight baseline before optimising
Execution (VWAP/TWAP, A/B testing) matters most when edge per share is small
Train on a minority of the data and walk forward out of sample on the rest; aim for ~1000 independent OOS predictions per feature
An ML filter layered on a simple signal (e.g. earnings surprise) can raise Sharpe by removing bad trades
High-Sharpe basket strategies come from many small-edge bets: trade win rates just over 50% but most days positive
notes: Process/ML episode. Common horizons cited: open-to-close, 1, 2 and 5 days. No concrete rule set given.

style: discretionary STIR relative-value / spread trader (Genesis Trading, 42 Trading)
markets: Australian short-term interest rate futures (bank bills, 3y/10y bonds)
edge_principles: Three-strikes rule: after three errors or lapses in standard (missed trade, miscalculation, needless scratch) stop trading for the session
Traders tend to work harder when doing badly and coast when doing well; pre-set rules should counter both
Write process rules in a calm, neutral state and phrase them constructively, not after a loss
Quarterly futures rollover brings in non-tick-sensitive participants forced to roll, creating short-term relative-value dislocations
During rollovers correlations decouple, so normal hedges can fail; a spread book can turn into an outright position
Big losses often follow long winning streaks and overconfidence; never try to win it all back fast while upset
Redundancy (UPS, generator, backup broker/PC, landline) is cheap insurance against operational losses
Wide tick sizes protected the market from HFT for a time; when competition becomes systematic, adapt toward quant methods
When in a slump, talk to traders who are doing well rather than ones who are also struggling
notes: Psychology/process episode about futures spread trading. No stock setup with rules.

style: performance psychology / trader development (ex-Mandara Capital performance director)
markets: oil and refined product derivatives (firm context)
edge_principles: Pick goals at the overlap of your strengths, interests and values; trading style should match personality and cognitive strengths
Test traits by putting candidates in realistic worst-case conditions; interviews mostly test interview skill
Watch error cascades: how many follow-on mistakes after the first one matters more than the first mistake
Improvement loop: define the aim (does it raise profit or cut risk?), map the current process and metrics, define a target state, then run small fast experiments against the biggest obstacle
Stretch targets (e.g. double the result with fewer resources) force new methods instead of doing a bit more of the same
Keep a stable routine so results can be tied to a strategy; change one thing at a time
Make desired behaviours the easiest option and add friction to bad ones
notes: Psychology/development episode. No trading setups.

style: crypto trader (Bitcoin and altcoins)
edge_principles: Exchange counterparty risk is real (hacks, DDoS, outages): keep only trading capital on exchanges, spread it out, and store the rest in hardware wallets
Exchange downtime or DDoS during a rally tends to kill the rally's momentum
Leverage lets traders keep fewer coins on an exchange, lowering custody exposure
Closed-end vehicles can trade far from NAV (GBTC was at roughly a 90% premium in mid-2017)
Frothy signs: a flood of new participants, ICOs raising money in seconds, 'missed the boat' buyers rotating into newer coins
notes: Crypto primer recorded June 2017. No rule-based setups.

style: journalist / author (Black Edge; ex-risk-arbitrage analyst)
edge_principles: Early edges were often structural and simple (1978 options arbitrage locking small spreads) and faded as competition arrived
Traits credited to Cohen's early trading: tape reading, reading how news moves prices, quick unemotional loss cutting
Others copying a successful trader erodes the edge, which pushes toward secrecy
Information edge must be legal; edge built on material non-public information ends in prosecution
Unusually consistent returns tend to draw regulator suspicion
notes: Story of the SAC Capital insider-trading case. No setups.

style: Treasury basis / relative-value trader (ex-Trans Market Group)
markets: US Treasury cash vs futures (10y, 30y), some S&P and euro futures
edge_principles: Execute without hesitation; a split-second delay can turn a winning arb into a loser
Cut losses fast; a loss that takes more than about a day to win back is too large
Daily profit target: once hit, stop for the day and come back fresh (take care of the short term)
Grow size only after building a capital cushion from successful runs
Paper trading cannot replace trading with real capital at risk
Fast competitors and resting-liquidity games mean size needs speed; without speed, move to longer-horizon relative-value trades where execution matters less
Long-term macro view can filter short-term trades, but the market can trade anywhere in the short run
Spreads, not outright direction, can be a trader's comfort zone; know which one fits you
notes: One relative-value bond setup is recorded. It is not testable with MCF stock data.

style: academic / calendar-anomaly and futures trader, Kelly sizing (Alpha Z Advisors)
markets: US index futures (S&P, Russell), Japanese equities (research), horse racing, sports betting
edge_principles: Start from a theory of money flows (paydays, institutional practice) before mining data for anomalies
Anomalies drift earlier as they get known (the January small-cap effect moved into December) and fade when big players copy them
No anomaly wins every year; judge by the long-run record, not one miss
Size by volatility; full Kelly is too violent for most, about half Kelly is a sensible default; multi-asset Kelly must be solved jointly, not name by name
Watch for becoming over-bet as conditions change even without new trades; correct quickly
Range mean reversion works a few times and then the range breaks; make sure the total is net positive
If a seasonal effect fails to show up in its usual pre-event window, read it as a warning sign
Start live with very small size after studying
notes: Several calendar setups; daily/index level; testable on SPY/IWM ETFs.

style: global macro plus intraday futures day trader (ex-RBC prop; The Macro Tourist)
markets: S&P futures, Bund/T-note futures, Euro Stoxx, long-dated index options, risk arb, convertibles
edge_principles: What is obvious is useless; if everyone is doing it, there is no money in it
Keep macro and intraday timeframes apart; do not let a losing day trade become a long-term holding, and trade the day's tape even against the macro view
Most of day trading is deciding which side to be on first; trading with the session bias keeps you on side even with poor entries
A small trader's edge lies at the extremes: deals so big they fill up the large players, or names too small for them to bother with
When hedge-fund positioning (CFTC COT) is crowded one way, fading it is often better than joining it
Look for the best way to express a view (e.g. long-dated options that also gain if rates rise)
Cut portfolio risk by adding offsetting or diversifying positions rather than only stops
Adapt to market-structure change (HFT, VWAP algos) instead of complaining
Journal and write to clarify thinking
notes: Intraday ORB+VWAP bias rule is testable on SPY. Macro trades are discretionary.

style: crypto OTC market maker (Cumberland Mining / DRW)
edge_principles: Apparent cross-exchange price gaps mostly reflect real frictions (jurisdiction, KYC, trading fees, fiat deposit/withdrawal costs) and are largely priced in
Counterparty and custody risk management is a core part of crypto trading
An edge in illiquid, opaque markets comes from mapping who the participants are and doing homework others skip
Block liquidity the exchanges cannot absorb is a niche for principal OTC desks
Judge new coins over a longer horizon and on utility, not one-day spikes
notes: Crypto market-structure episode. No setups.

style: biographer (Claude Shannon, A Mind at Play)
edge_principles: Shannon's real investing returns (about 24% compounded, by the account given) came from a few early-stage holdings in companies whose founders he knew, held for decades
Fundamental checks: good management, good product; try the product and meet the founders
Rebalancing between cash and a volatile asset can in theory harvest volatility, but commissions can erase it
Broad curiosity and hands-on tinkering helped creative problem solving
notes: Biography episode. Records the volatility-harvesting rebalancing idea as a low-confidence setup.

style: global macro hedge fund manager (Fourth Turning Capital; MacroVoices host)
markets: crude oil, US dollar index, rates, broad macro
edge_principles: Learn to run your own money rather than handing it to high-fee private wealth products; avoid illiquid long-lockup commitments that can force fire sales
Pick a style that fits your personality and that you enjoy, since the edge comes from out-working others (Market Wizards as a style survey)
Long-cycle themes (Fourth Turning, peak cheap oil, reserve-currency change) choose which markets to study, but trades can run opposite the long-term thesis in the near term
Long-dated futures matter: a spot low with high deferred prices is not the same opportunity as a whole curve that is cheap
Do not anchor on post-WWII-only history; use longer cycles
notes: Macro-theme episode recorded August 2017. No rule-based setups.
